item.title: How Does an Autistic Brain Learn to Recognize Faces?
item.description: A new study using EEG brain scans found that autistic children's brains process faces differently than neurotypical children — and those differences may begin much earlier than scientists thought.

item.title: How Did Scientists Discover New Animals in a Lab, Airport, Cemetery, and Parking Lot?
item.description: From a neuroscience lab tank to a parking lot patch of moss, scientists are finding new species where we least expect them — even in our own backyards.

item.title: How Did a Luxury Cruise Ship End Up Stranded in Cambodia After Soaring Fuel Costs?
item.description: The Villa Vie Odyssey was more than 750 days into a 3.5-year journey around the world when rising fuel costs forced it to suspend operations in Cambodia.

item.title: 10 Amazing Animals Discovered in Places You'd Least Expect
item.description: From laboratory tanks to airport runways, new animal species turn up where we live, work, and travel — sometimes right under our noses.

item.title: How did a stretch of Antarctic water get named after a BBC science reporter?
item.description: A channel of water between two Antarctic islands now carries the name of Jonathan Amos, a BBC science correspondent who reported on polar research for nearly four decades.

item.title: How did four astronauts travel 100 million miles and come home safely?
item.description: After spending 237 days living and working aboard the International Space Station, four international astronauts safely splashed down in their Crew Dragon capsule — closing a mission that traveled more than 100 million miles around Earth.

item.title: How Did Tanzania Find Its First New Natural Gas in Over a Decade?
How Did a Teacher's Daily Positivity Practice Spread Through an Elementary School?
item.description: A first-grade teacher in Kansas started a simple daily affirmation circle — now children across every grade at Rex Elementary are ending their school day feeling confident and kind.

item.title: How does a lava planet keep its atmosphere? James Webb spots a giant sunscreen
item.description: A scorching rocky world 280 light-years away should have lost its atmosphere long ago — yet the James Webb Space Telescope finds it still reflects about 75% of its star's light, possibly because of silicate clouds acting like a giant sunscreen.

item.title: How Did Scientists Find New Animals Hiding in Airports, Cemeteries, and Labs?
item.description: From aquarium tanks to apartment parking lots, a transparent fish in a lab, a Darth Vader isopod in seafood markets, and a legless lizard at LAX — scientists keep discovering new species in the most ordinary corners of our world.

item.title: The Site Is Live — How This Page Was Published
item.description: This article is a pipeline test: written on a VPS, built by a script, and pushed to GitHub Pages — no human touched it.

item.title: How Do Our Immune Cells 'Feel' the World Around Them With a Hidden Sense of Touch?
item.description: Immune cells called T cells can sense how stiff or soft the tissues around them are, using this 'hidden sense of touch' to decide whether to become long-term guardians that stay in the body's tissues. The discovery, published in Nature Immunology, shows that these cells use physical cues from their environment — not just chemical signals — to shape how they protect us.

item.title: Can AI really be trusted to do science on its own?
item.description: AI is racing through maths, biology and crystal-hunting — but a growing number of scientists worry that speed comes at a cost: a crisis of trust. Can we tell real discovery from AI-generated fiction?

item.title: How Did a Dartmouth High School Baseball Team Stay Smiling Through 6 Winless Seasons?
item.description: The Dartmouth High School Spartans in Nova Scotia haven't won a baseball game in six years — yet every player still shows up with cheer, cleats, and a paint-stained smile. Their secret? No cut roster means everyone gets a turn, and the team's 'vibes guy' makes sure the fun never fades.

item.title: How Did a Wrong Turn Save 14 Lives From a Burning House in Georgia?
item.description: A stranger's wrong turn in Georgia led him straight to a house fire where he helped rescue 14 children belonging to a foster family that has cared for over 500 kids.

item.title: How Did Early Humans Reach the Jordan Valley 1.9 Million Years Ago?
item.description: A 1.9-million-year-old archaeological site in Israel's Jordan Valley shows that early humans left Africa hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists once thought. Three advanced dating methods converged on the same surprising timeline, pushing back the story of our species' first steps into the Middle East.

item.title: How Did Knitted Traffic Cops Help Slow Down Speeding Drivers in a Quiet English Village?
item.description: In the village of Fillongley, Warwickshire, a group of crafty knitters created life-sized woolen traffic officers and speed cameras to slow down speeding drivers — and it's working!

item.title: What happened when a Nanotyrannus skeleton sold for $47.3 million?
item.description: A rare skeleton of Nanotyrannus, a dinosaur once mistaken for a teenage T. rex, sold for $47.3 million at auction — sparking a debate over whether priceless fossils should live in museums or private vaults.

item.title: How Did a Hidden Crystal Patchwork Sabotage a Superconductor Studied for 40 Years?
item.description: Scientists peering inside a copper-based superconductor that has been studied for four decades made a stunning discovery: the crystal is not uniform at all. It is a patchwork of different atomic arrangements stitched together by surprisingly wide boundary zones that may quietly weaken the very superconductivity researchers have been trying to understand and improve.

item.title: How Did an Asteroid That Killed the Dinosaurs Help Ants Conquer the World?
item.description: 66 million years ago, an asteroid slammed into Earth and ended the age of the dinosaurs. In the aftermath, 'jumping genes' in ant DNA surged into action — giving ants a surprise genetic boost that may explain why they became the world's most successful group of social insects.
